The Patriots got wide receiver A.J. Brown back last week, but also lost a wide receiver, with Romeo Dobbs going on IR with a shoulder injury. The team will also be without CB Carlton Davis (neck) for another week, while OT Morgan Moses (foot) is among those questionable.

On the Bears side, running back Kyle Monangai and linebacker Jack Sanborn were ruled out ahead of the game and DB Tyrique Stevenson (hip) is their one questionable player, with LB T.J. Edwards (hamstring) doubtful.

Notable from Wednesday's injury report include Baltimore Ravens QB Lamar Jackson (ankle) was limited in practice, Tampa Bay Buccaneers QB Baker Mayfield (right thumb) was a full participant, and New York Jets RB Breece Hall (quad) was a non-participant.

text:
The 1-5 Tampa Bay Buccaneers head to Charlotte in Week Seven to take on the team at the top of their division standings and the reigning NFC South champs, the 3-2 Carolina Panthers. The Buccaneers will try to duplicate their road success from Week Five, when they excelled in all three phases in a 24-16 win in Dallas. Kickoff on Sunday is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET at Bank of America Stadium, with FOX handling the local broadcast.

The Buccaneers were unable to maintain their momentum from that win in Dallas last weekend, surrendering a 16-3 fourth-quarter lead in what would turn into an overtime battle won by the visiting Pittsburgh Steelers, 26-19. Until the game slipped away in the fourth quarter and overtime, there were plenty of encouraging developments, including the emergence of anreinvigorated pass rush that was one of the main line items on the team's offseason plan. David Walker had two more sacks as he continued to make a weekly impact in his first season of action, rookies Rueben Bain Jr. and Keionte Scott each tallied their first career sacks and veteran Al-Quadin Muhammad got his first as a Buccaneer. Jalon Daniels and the Bucs' offense put together an impressive, methodical touchdown drive in the second quarter but subsequently had to settle for field goals too many times.

Carolina took care of business without much trouble in Philadelphia in Week Six against an Eagles squad that was missing Jalen Hurts, Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith, Landon Dickerson and the recently retired Lane Johnson. The Panthers stung a talented, if also banged-up, Eagles defense for 399 yards, including 281 passing by Bryce Young and 120 on the ground by running back Chuba Hubbard. Carolina's defense got to fill-in quarterback Tanner McKee for three sacks and held the Eagles' rushing attack to just 35 yards and 2.7 yards per carry. Carolina has gradually been able to stock a talented group of skill-position players around Bryce Young, including Hubbard (511 yards from scrimmage), Tetairoa McMillan (471 receiving yards) and Jalen Coker, who returned from missing a game with a quad injury and immediately hauled in six receptions for 97 yards against the Eagles. Carolina's defense is 25th in yards allowed and 21st in points allowed and currently has its starting cornerback duo of Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson on injured reserve, but free agency additions Devin Lloyd and Jaelen Phillips are paying off nicely.

Here are four major storylines as well as four head-to-head player battles to keep an eye on as the Bucs square off against the Panthers on Sunday afternoon:

TOP STORYLINES

Division Play Begins – It admittedly feels a bit distasteful to be talking about the playoff race with a 1-5 Bucs team, but the basic reality of the situation is that Tampa Bay has a clear path to get back in the NFC South race if it can start winning some of the one-score games that have become their norm. And that is particularly true in regards to the six games the Buccaneers have left against their three division foes, starting with the Panthers on Sunday. Now at 3-2, Carolina has created a clear gap in the standings, 1.5 games ahead of Atlanta and New Orleans and 2.5 ahead of the Buccaneers. Whether or not the Panthers are also clearly demonstrating that they are the class of the division will start to be answered now that more intra-division games are on tap.The same is true of the Buccaneers, who have had trouble finishing games but believe they will be able to prove they are significantly better than their record suggests. Head Coach Todd Bowles told his team after the Week Six loss to Pittsburgh that the season is not lost, but that the team no longer has any margin for error. Losses in upcoming games to either the Panthers or Falcons, or both, would make that margin razor thin.

Which Offense Shows Up for Bucs? – The Buccaneers have played their last three games with undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels at the offensive helm thanks to the dislocated right thumb sustained by Baker Mayfield in Week Three. While those three games including the sort of ups and downs one would expect from an offense led by an inexperienced rookie passer, the team did appear to find a formula for success for that unit in its Week Five win in Dallas. That started with a 241-yard rushing attack paced by Bucky Irving, and while that admittedly came against one of the league's poorest run defenses, the Panthers also rank 27th in run defense (and last in yards allowed per carry) and might offer the same opportunity for the Bucs to succeed with a run-heavy script. Tampa Bay's offensive line opened big holes for Irving in Dallas and also allowed only one sack, all of which helped Daniels stay in control and avoid putting the ball in harm's way, with no turnovers. Against the Steelers, Daniels was sacked five times and intercepted twice and the Bucs couldn't lean on the run game, with Irving held to 46 yards on 19 carries. Which version of the Bucs' offense from the past two weeks will show up in Charlotte, and will it be Daniels under center or Mayfield in a return to the lineup?

Containing the Young Gun – After a rough start to his career that saw him get benched early in his second season, the Panthers' youthful quarterback, Bryce Young, made steady progression under Dave Canales in the second half of 2024 and all of last season. In his fourth year, however, young has gone from that steady improvement to a full-on blossom into one of the league's most productive passers. He leads the NFL with 309.8 passing yards per game and has tossed 11 touchdowns against two interceptions. Notably, young has been able to push the ball downfield, ranking third in big passing plays, according to StatsPass, with 15. Young also has good mobility, and while he has only run nine times for 25 yards through five games this year, he is able to extend plays and look for McMillan and Coker downfield. The play of the Buccaneers' secondary has been perhaps the most pleasant surprise for the team in the midst of its series of losses, with Zyon McCollum, Jacob Parrish and Keionte Scott all posting favorable coverage numbers. If Tampa Bay's run defense, which is currently ranked second in the NFL, continues to excel, the Panthers may have to put most of the offensive workload on Young's shoulders, and the Bucs will need to keep him from having a big day in order to leave Charlotte with a win.

Has the Promised Pass Rush Arrived? – After two straight games without a sack, the Bucs' defense exploded for five of them against the Steelers, which was the sort of production the team thought was possible after adding Rueben Bain Jr. and Al-Quadin Muhammad and getting David Walker back from injury. Those three combined to record 4.0 sacks of Aaron Rodgers, who was also hit 10 times in the game. Carolina's offense ranks 15th in the league, so in the middle of the pack, in terms of sacks allowed per pass rate and Young has gone down 12 times through five games. Is this a matchup the Buccaneers can get on the right side of in Week Seven? Will the five-sack outburst in Week Six prove to be a proof of concept and the start of a weekly run ofcausing big-time pressure, or will it prove to be the outlier in the early part of the season?

KEY MATCHUPS

1. Panthers T Rasheed Walker vs. Buccaneers OLB David Walker

David Walker is on a heater for the Buccaneers, recording a team-high 4.0 sacks, including two last week plus three QB hits against the Steelers. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, among players with at least 45 pass-rush snaps, Walker ranks first in sack rate (8.2%), first in QB hit rate (12.2%), second in pressure rate (28.6%) and third in quick pressure rate (12.2%). That Walker's sack ranking is higher than his pressure ranking suggests that, unlike some of the Bucs' otherpass rushers this season, when he is finding his way to the vicinity of the quarterback he is frequently finishing the job of getting him to the ground. Walker, who had a school-record 31.0 sacks and 63.0 tackles for loss in three seasons at Central Arkansas but then missed his rookie NFL campaign due to a knee injury, is finding that his quick first snap, instant acceleration to the quarterback and vision for rush lanes is translating well to the NFL. He has rushed from both ends of the Bucs' line and has seen his reps increase week to week as he continues to produce, so it is very likely he will spend some time engaged with left tackle Rasheed Walker. The Panthers signed Walker to a one-year deal in free agency after he had three nice seasons with the Packers, and they needed him to at least bridge the gap until the return of Ikem Ekwonu from a ruptured patellar tendon suffered in the playoffs last year. The 6-6, 328-pound Walker is an imposing figure who will have a significant size advantage on Walker but could struggle to win the leverage battle. He is a powerful blocker in the run game and a strong anchor against bull rushes.

2. Buccaneers RB Bucky Irving vs. Panthers LB Devin Lloyd

Bucky Irving may be the key to the Bucs' rebounding on offense after that unit had an uneven performance against Pittsburgh. Irving recently ran for 165 yards in a win at Dallas and his 72-yard breakaway in that contest put all of his freakish talents on display as he wound through the Cowboys' defense and left multiple defenders in his wake. Irving has played the Panthers four times in his young career and has averaged 136.0 yards from scrimmage in those contests. This time around, he will face a Carolina defense that is last in the NFL in yards allowed per carry, at 5.12. Even so, the Panthers are surely very happy with their big free agency investment in linebacker Devin Lloyd, who leads the Panthers with 35 tackles and also has 2.0 sacks, four tackles for loss and four quarterback hits. The Buccaneers would like to get Irving going again in the passing game, but in that area he'll probably see a lot of Lloyd, who has already broken up three passes this season. Lloyd's breakthrough season in Jacksonville in 2025 included five interceptions, and so far he has proven that to be no fluke, picking off two more passes in his first five games in Carolina.

3. Panthers WR Tetairoa McMillan vs. Buccaneers CB Zyon McCollum

Tetairoa McMillan, who was the eighth pick in the draft in 2025, won the Offensive Rookie of the Year award in his debut campaign and has shown no signs of slowing down in 2026. McMillan leads the Panthers with 32 receptions for 471 yards and is tied for ninth in receiving yards in the NFL despite the Panthers already having their bye week. In the predraft process last year, McMillan was often compared to Mike Evans but with the added ability to generate a lot of yards after the catch. The former Arizona star has a big frame and a huge catch radius and is nails in contested-catch situations, but he also moves very fluidly for his size. The Panthers have significantly increased his percentage in the slot this season over his rookie year, which is news that should be delivered to Keionte Scott, but he will still see plenty of action on the outside and will run into a cornerback in Zyon McCollum who is also having a very strong season. McCollum has the size and the speed to match up with McMillan on any route and in any situation and he is playing with the kind of unshakable confidence that is key for his position. From Weeks Three to Five, McCollum played 104 coverage snaps and only allowed two receptions. A one-on-one battle between McCollum and McMillan could turn into a classic rivalry in the years to come between the two division foes.

4. Buccaneers G Cody Mauch vs. Panthers DT Derrick Brown

The Panthers' run defense has struggled a bit in the early going of the 2026 season, but it would be in a much tougher spot without the powerful Derrick Brown in the middle of its front. After missing almost all of 2024 with a knee injury, Brown returned last year to record 46 run stops for an improved Carolina defense, which ranked fourth among defensive tackles. Since 2022, Brown has 175 run stops, which ranks second among defensive tackles in that span despite the lost 2024 campaign. Brown also has three quarterback pressures, and he knows when to give up on his rush and get his hands up in the passing lanes, as his four passes defensed suggest. Cody Mauch should get a big dose of big Derrick Brown on Sunday and will need to be able to move him so the Bucs can get their run game going. The Bucs' fourth-year guard is a battler who has returned from a season-ending knee injury in 2025 to establish himself as part of a line that showed off its dominant 2024 form two weeks ago against Dallas.

text:
The Denver Broncos hit the practice field on Wednesday as they begin on-field preparations for Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals.

Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain (ankle) and wide receiver Jaylen Waddle (chest) were limited while safety Talanoa Hufanga (ankle), outside linebacker Jonah Elliss (ankle) and running back Tyler Badie (thumb) did not participate.

Denver outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper (reinstated last week) and running back Jonah Coleman (ankle) returned to practice, and cornerback Riley Moss (ribs) was a full participant.

Surtain has missed the team's last two games, and it sounds like he might also miss Week 7, but returning to practice is a good step in the right direction. Hufanga is likely going to miss at least one more game after sitting out last week's contest. Jahdae Barron and Taylor Rapp have done a nice job stepping up in the secondary while PS2 and Hufanga have been sidelined.

Elliss limped off the field late in the fourth quarter of last Thursday's game, and he was spotted wearing a walking boot and using crutches at a Colorado-Utah game two days later. It looks like Elliss will be sidelined for a bit after he wrote "Be right back" on social media over the weekend.

Denver coach Sean Payton indicated Elliss avoided a season-ending injury, but he seemed to hint that Elliss could land on short-term injured reserve later this week. Meanwhile, Cooper is expected to return to the active roster this week after being reinstated by the NFL.

Badie injured his thumb in the second quarter of last Thursday's game, and he was ruled out just before halftime. Meanwhile, Coleman is eligible to return from injured reserve this week, and he returned to practice on Wednesday, opening his 21-day window to be activated to the 53-man roster.

Denver's scheduled to practice again on Thursday and Friday before releasing a final injury report with game statuses for Sunday.

Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak said the 2025 fourth-round is still in the NFL's concussion protocol. He was hurt in Week 5 and he didn't play in a Week 6 loss to the Buffalo Bills. Monday, Kubiak said he was expecting Hemingway back in practice this week. If he returns to practice by Friday, he can still have a chance to face the Rams.

Hemingway has been the Raiders' snap leader at defensive tackle. He averaged playing 62 percent of the snaps in the four games he was fully healthy for. Foley Fatukasi started in place of Hemingway against the Bills.

Meanwhile, Kubiak said second-year wide receiver Dont'e Thornton has a chance to be activated from the injured reserve this week, but the coach indicated Thornton has to show he's ready. He must be activated by next week or he would be out for the season.

Kubiak also said there will be competition on the offensive line again this week. Caleb Rogers replaced Jackson Powers-Johnson in Week 6.

title: Lions to get DB Brian Branch C Cade Mays back vs Packers - ESPN
authors: Eric Woodyard, Jeff Legwold, Rob Demovsky, DJ Bien-Aime, Tim McManus, Field Yates, Mel Kiper Jr, Jordan Reid, Jeremy Fowler, Dan Graziano
description:
DETROIT -- Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell was growing tired of hearing his star defensive back Brian Branch plead his case for when he should return to the field.
As the Lions prepare to host the Green Bay Packers in their first NFC North battle of the 2026 season, both Branch and center Cade Mays are expected to suit up.
"Barring anything negatively happening between now and the game, we plan on playing both of those guys," Campbell said of Branch and Mays on Monday.
The Lions officially opened the 21-day practice windows for Branch (Achilles) and Mays (wrist) ahead of the bye week on Oct. 7.
Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is also itching to work Branch back into the rotation.
text:
DETROIT -- Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell was growing tired of hearing his star defensive back Brian Branch plead his case for when he should return to the field. After a 10-month absence, Branch is finally in position to receive his wish this week.

As the Lions prepare to host the Green Bay Packers in their first NFC North battle of the 2026 season, both Branch and center Cade Mays are expected to suit up.

"Barring anything negatively happening between now and the game, we plan on playing both of those guys," Campbell said of Branch and Mays on Monday.

The Lions officially opened the 21-day practice windows for Branch (Achilles) and Mays (wrist) ahead of the bye week on Oct. 7.

Although the defense was struggling, and Branch was pressing the issue, Campbell and the medical staff refused to rush him back into action until they felt he was fully ready.

"I told Dan like, 'I'm starving' since I got injured," Branch said. "Just been day by day. Just been working, just been grinding. Showing up at 7 a.m."

Branch, 24, was placed on the reserve/PUP list, meaning he would miss at least the first four games of the season after suffering a season-ending Achilles injury in 2025 that sidelined him throughout training camp and the preseason.

He suffered the torn Achilles in Week 14 during the fourth quarter of the Lions' 44-30 win over the Dallas Cowboys and had to be carted off the field. He underwent surgery last December and his recovery period was projected to take eight to 12 months.

Even with him being back, the Lions will try to remain conservative with his workload on Sunday after being away for so long.

"Yeah, I think that'd be asking a lot to say he's going to play 70 plays, but we do feel like he can handle quite a bit here and we're going to push him in practice here early," Campbell said.

Detroit will benefit from Branch's presence after the defense gave up at least 30 points in three of its first four games.

Although the unit enjoyed a much better performance against Arizona on Oct. 11, the biggest struggles have been in the secondary where they've given up a league-high 1,487 passing yards. Branch feels he's "ready to go" after shaking off the rust during practice and remains confident he can help.

"I just know what these group of guys are made up of and we all want the same thing. We all got the same goal," Branch said. "And we know that we've been shooting ourselves in the foot and shoot, we go hard each and every day. ... if you've got hard work, you're going to overcome a lot of things."

Branch, a 2024 Pro Bowler, was drafted by the Lions in the second round of the 2023 NFL draft out of Alabama. He is eligible for a contract extension while playing on the final season of his rookie deal.

In 2025, Branch started in all 12 of his appearances, logging 75 tackles, nine passes defended and five quarterback hits as one of the team's top defenders. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is also itching to work Branch back into the rotation.

"Listen, I don't even know the word for it. I don't. But I mean, how many positions can he play and how fast?" Sheppard said. "I mean, he's a dynamic player. That is an elite player in this league, which we all know, guys. I'm not telling you nothing you don't know. That is an elite player in this league. But we also got to do right by the player."

Mays suffered his wrist injury during training camp and was placed on injured reserve. He was projected to miss eight to 10 weeks and is on track to reenter the mix. Mays was acquired during the offseason to help the offensive line after spending his first four seasons with the Carolina Panthers. Campbell this week confirmed that Mays will likely start at center against the Packers although veteran OL Juice Scruggs has played well in his absence. Mays went through practice with quality reps and Campbell feels comfortable with bringing him back in that starting role, while Scruggs will swing between center and guard.

"We would like to just rip this Band-Aid off of Cade," Campbell told 97.1 The Ticket on Wednesday morning. "I thought he had some good work yesterday. I thought he looked pretty good."

With the Lions at 3-2, Campbell feels the returns have the team in good shape as it enters its first divisional matchup this season.

Detroit went 2-4 against NFC North opponents last season after going 15-3 from 2022-24, which was tied with the Chiefs for the best intra-division record in the NFL, per ESPN Research.

"I mean, we already kind of have a range of what we're looking at for him and for Cade a little bit," Campbell said. "We're still back and forth on what do we do with him? Do we work he and Juice in and out? In the center position, that's where it's a little different than a guard. That's somebody that's constantly touching the football."

text:
CHICAGO -- The Bears will be without running back Kyle Monangai against the New England Patriots in Week 7.

Monangai did not practice in any of the Bears walk-throughs ahead of Thursday night's game at Soldier Field and is set to miss his third straight game with turf toe and thumb injuries.

The Bears lead the NFL with 161 rushing yards per game but were held below 100 in consecutive games with Monangai sidelined. The former seventh rounder is averaging 5.4 yards per rush, which is the fourth most in the NFL behind Kenneth Walker III (6.3), Bijan Robinson (5.8) and Jaylen Warren (5.5).

Chicago was averaging 6.8 yards per play with Monangai on the field, a figure that has dipped to 4.7 without him.

Monangai produced a career-high 30 carries for 146 yards and two touchdowns in the Bears' 23-12 win over the Jets in Week 4. He exited that game late in the fourth quarter with a thumb injury, but it wasn't until the following week that he appeared on the injury report with a toe injury.

Coach Ben Johnson said Monangai's toe injury was a "bigger deal" than the team initially anticipated, which prompted a visit to a specialist for further evaluation. The running back was then categorized by Johnson as "week-to-week."

Last Friday, Johnson intimated that the Monangai's absence should not be longer than four games, the mandated amount a player would miss with an injured reserve designation.

"It wasn't one of those things we felt like we needed to put him on IR for," Johnson said on Oct.16. "So, it's still week to week and as far as I know, he's trending in the right direction."

In five of its six games, New England has had held opponents below 100 rushing yards.

text:
SANTA CLARA -- Uh oh.

Mykel Williams seems to have re-injured his surgically repaired knee during the 49ers' Week 6 win over the Washington Commanders.

Williams seemed fine after the game. But today, head coach Kyle Shanahan mentioned that Williams has a knee injury and listed him among the players who would not participate in Wednesday's practice. When asked if Williams' surgically repaired knee "flared up" on Monday night during the game, Shanahan said, "Just knee," meaning that's all the information he was required to divulge.

It sounds like Williams did indeed re-aggravate his knee during the game on Monday night. If Shanahan could have provided some reassuring nugget of information, he probably would have, but he didn't. He allowed us to use our imaginations, which usually is a bad sign.

Williams tore his ACL on Nov. 2 last year. He missed all of training camp and the first four games of this season as he recovered as quickly as possible. As soon as he was eligible to be activated from the Physically Unable to Perform List, the 49ers activated him. That was two weeks ago.

Since then, Williams has come off the bench as a rotational defensive lineman and played fewer than 50 percent of the time. Clearly, he was not quite ready to play, even though he recorded his second career sack on Monday against the Commanders. The 49ers were trying to manage him prudently.

And Williams still re-injured his knee. That's disconcerting.

In hindsight, the 49ers once again allowed a player to play before he should have. I'm guessing the 49ers asked Williams if he felt ready to go, and he said yes, as almost any professional football player would say. They're programmed to want to play no matter what.

That's why teams have to protect players from themselves. You've heard that cliché a million times because it's true. Teams must prevent players from making shortsighted decisions. Teams have to be the ones who consider the big picture and worry about the long haul.

The 49ers don't do a good enough job of protecting players from themselves. Just last week, the 49ers let Mike Evans play through Achilles tendinitis, and he made it worse. Earlier in the season, they let Nick Bosa return from his third ACL tear before he had completed a full practice, and he wound up injuring his calf.

When players come back too early, they often reinjure themselves. If anyone should understand that by now, it's the 49ers.

When will they realize that they have to be more careful?

text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Rams linebacker Nate Landman has entered the NFL's concussion protocol in yet another injury setback for slumping Los Angeles.

Coach Sean McVay said Landman will miss Wednesday's practice after getting hurt in the Rams' 18-16 loss to Arizona last Sunday.

Landman is the Rams' leader with 51 tackles, including two for loss. He has also forced two fumbles while serving as the Rams' primary defensive signal-caller.

The Rams (2-4) travel to face the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday after losing three of their past four games in a season they began as Super Bowl favorites.

If Landman can't play, the Rams would be without their top tackler along with All-Pro defensive tackle Myles Garrett, who hasn't played since Week 1 because of knee surgery, and run-stopping defensive linemen Kobie Turner and Poona Ford, who both got hurt against the Cardinals.

McVay also said star cornerback Trent McDuffie will miss Wednesday's practice after missing the game against Arizona with a groin injury. The Rams won't determine his availability for Las Vegas until later in the week.

The Rams already know they will be without six-time Pro Bowl receiver Davante Adams for at least the next six to 10 weeks after he injured his hamstring on a noncontact play late in LA's loss to Arizona. But McVay said the Rams aren't looking to acquire a receiver to fill the hole left by Adams, who led the NFL in touchdown catches last season.

“We’ve got some depth on the roster,” McVay said.

The 33-year-old Adams has 30 receptions for 480 yards and four TDs already this season, stepping up particularly during a two-game injury absence for All-Pro wideout Puka Nacua.

Adams had surgery Tuesday to repair a torn hamstring tendon, but it's unclear how quickly he can return for the rest of his 13th NFL season.

“Just disappointed for him,” NFL MVP Matthew Stafford said. “I know how hard he works to keep his body feeling as good as it can, and how hard he works to be out there for us. When he's not able to do that, I know that tears him up. The production is the production. He's an unbelievable player. Has been for a long time in this league.”

The Rams' third-leading wide receiver this season is Konata Mumpfield, who has only eight catches for 127 yards. McVay indicated that the 2025 seventh-round pick, who had only 10 catches as a rookie last season, will have more chances to contribute.

“What I do appreciate is he's made the most out of his opportunities,” McVay said. “There's just been less chances to be able to contribute. He's one of those guys that when he's been counted on, he's delivered. He's mature for a younger player, really curious, got a great humility about himself.”

title: Jalen Hurts' health shouldn't be up for debate - Andscape
description:
The NFL may have decided not to punish the Philadelphia Eagles, but the team still fumbled Jalen Hurts’ health.
“It looked like they were trying to pin the outcome of this season on Jalen Hurts,” Robinson noted, “just so that they can have an excuse later on to move on from Jalen Hurts.” Then came the devil’s advocacy.
'” Robinson issued a social media apology Monday, saying his comments were “unfounded” and he “never should have speculated” on Hurts’ health or “commitment to his team.” Jalen Hurts has long been one of the most polarizing names in sports.
That’s Jalen Hurts’ football experience in a nutshell.
Jalen Hurts, a Black man, is a 28-year-old NFL starting quarterback with every presumed medical option available … and it still almost went left.
text:
The NFL may have decided not to punish the Philadelphia Eagles, but the team still fumbled Jalen Hurts’ health.

When the Philadelphia starting quarterback called his calf injury a “very unique experience” last week, the first red flag appeared. However, it’s not about what comes next for the former Super Bowl MVP, who is now out for the year. The more troubling question is what the Eagles risked to preserve what little hope they had left in the season.

The league and the Eagles would much rather fast-forward to the Week 7 slate Sunday — or Monday night, in the Eagles’ case — than dwell on the Hurts saga.

Right or wrong, actual football is an elixir to the game’s inevitable controversies. The NFL attempted to close the door, informing the NFLPA it wouldn’t be punishing the Eagles or reviewing protocol as a result of how Hurts’ care was handled. On Tuesday night, the NFLPA kicked that same door in, demanding a “full investigation into what occurred.”

Yet, before that…

The eeriness of a hospital room in the dead of night lives with a person. People live there. Family trees alter there. People die there — in many cases due to circumstances beyond their control. Complete darkness is only disrupted by hallway light seeping in through the bottom of the door. Or a curtain, depending on the setup. Only the sounds of machines monitoring vital signs break the silence.

Maybe a light was on here. Maybe doctors interrupted the machines’ beeps while keeping tabs on a high-profile patient. Regardless, such was Hurts’ reality in London earlier this month.

The Eagles’ franchise quarterback sat in a hospital, per NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, until 3 a.m. after being told not to sleep because of the risk of a blood clot. How did the team respond to Hurts’ safety already being in jeopardy? He then played the entire game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Rapoport called the scenario “crazy.”

In reality, it’s far darker.

It’s asinine. It’s inhumane. It’s life-or-death. And it’s a decision that should carry serious consequences.

The timeline is the indictment, and the Eagles’ medical staff is directly in the crosshairs. Hurts took a cleat to the calf during the Eagles’ Oct. 4 loss to the Rams. Six days later, he was diagnosed with a superficial clot, and eventually went 21-of-40 passing against the Jaguars in London.

Sources told Rapoport that Hurts was able to sleep approximately seven hours at the team hotel and napped until taking the field for pregame warmups.

Barely a full day in London, but evidently enough time to diagnose a clot and clear him to play.

Over the next several days, Hurts’ clot moved — though the Eagles never specified how much. That turned out to be the worst answer. Hurts was shut down, moved to injured reserve and ultimately ruled out for the season. The official diagnosis was deep vein thrombosis (DVT) along with bilateral pulmonary emboli — requiring at minimum three months on blood thinners.

In less than a week, Hurts’ condition went from “superficial” to clots in both lungs and questions about what the rest of his career — one of the most dissected and debated in recent sports history — will be. But it also begs questions that have become increasingly impossible to ignore.

What did “medically cleared” look like during those dark, early morning hours in London? And what’s the protocol for a superficial clot?

When it comes to pulmonary embolisms, aka “blood clots,” sudden death is the “first symptom” and occurs in about 25 percent of cases. Roughly two-thirds of deaths happen within two hours — making Hurts’ initial “superficial” diagnosis all the more harrowing.

Pulmonary embolisms, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, mark a leading cause of preventable hospital deaths. Clots often disguise themselves as rib injuries, fatigue or calf strains — all common costs of doing business playing professional football. It’s a blitz no one sees coming, not even those whose job it is to decipher them.

Black Americans, in particular, experience far more frequent battles with this reality. Compared to white Americans, Black Americans have 30- to 60-percent higher fatality rates and are three times more likely to die from a blood clot outside a hospital — and have higher odds to die within 30 days of diagnosis. Roughly a third of people with recent DVT’s say they experienced barriers to treatment, citing awareness, cost, racial bias and more.

There are the numbers. Then the words. The Eagles’ 2-4 start has laid blame at the feet of a litany of individuals and parties within the organization — Hurts, fairly and unfairly, being the most obvious of them all. All while his blood was literally clotting.

Last Thursday on NFL Network, Michael Robinson, a former Pro Bowl fullback, insinuated Hurts’ blood clot meant he quit on his teammates. First came the organizational blame.

“It looked like they were trying to pin the outcome of this season on Jalen Hurts,” Robinson noted, “just so that they can have an excuse later on to move on from Jalen Hurts.”

Then came the devil’s advocacy.

“‘If everybody’s hurt, I’m hurt too,’” he said, speaking hypothetically from Hurts’ perspective. “[Maybe he’s] getting himself out of the fray so that this lost season. … He’s pulling himself off so that this doesn’t look like ‘It’s on me.'”

Robinson issued a social media apology Monday, saying his comments were “unfounded” and he “never should have speculated” on Hurts’ health or “commitment to his team.”

Jalen Hurts has long been one of the most polarizing names in sports. When his team wins, the credit goes to the offensive line, skill position players and stout defense. When he loses, it’s because of his perceived inability to maximize such amenities. The truth has always existed in the gray area in between.

Robinson’s comments, however, reflect the grace football inevitably erodes. It’s a game where failure is far more prevalent than success, but a player who fails to meet the expected ratio of success becomes the enemy. That’s Jalen Hurts’ football experience in a nutshell.

That’s why the analysis of Hurts’ situation — without sleep for nearly two days, according to The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero, and ailing in a hospital only to be released to play an NFL game — became so unnerving.

He was said to be ducking accountability. As a Black man playing the most scrutinized position in American sports, he somehow lacked the fortitude it required to play — as if footage of him being benched in the 2018 college football national championship game, a nightmare scenario he handled with grace and bounced back from to become a Super Bowl champion, hadn’t been released days before.

There’s a long tradition in football of treating a Black quarterback’s injury as a character referendum first and a medical event second. Robinson couched it as devil’s advocacy. But speculation doesn’t need malice to do damage — it just needs a platform.

Jalen Hurts, a Black man, is a 28-year-old NFL starting quarterback with every presumed medical option available … and it still almost went left. Now imagine that same clot in a different body that wasn’t as consistently analyzed as the franchise quarterback’s. Imagine if he was your bartender, your hair stylist, or the one delivering your Amazon packages.

Blood clots are no strangers to sports. Mike Williams, a former offensive lineman for the Washington Commanders, experienced one in the summer of 2010. He never played again.

The stark precedent, though, is Basketball Hall of Famer and two-time NBA champion Chris Bosh. About a decade ago, I begged him to retire from basketball for many of the same reasons Hurts faces now. His initial February 2015 clot was, surprise surprise, mistaken for a rib injury. He returned months later and played until February 2016, when a second clot appeared in his leg.

His career, which included 11 All-Star Games and the most important block, rebound and assist in Miami Heat history, was over at 31 … for the same issues that the Eagles allowed Hurts to play through.

Nuance is added when you consider the society in which all of this is unfolding. Hurts is an American citizen; a country constantly at war with itself over healthcare just witnessed an uncomfortable case study.

The joint statement from the Eagles and Hurts’ agent Nicole Lynn is commendable. Though it embodied transparency, it still begs the question: Why did the Eagles feel comfortable putting a player on the field who hadn’t had adequate rest following an international flight, even with approval from doctors in London?

Grace is afforded when empathy lives in the proverbial courtroom. Football’s track record is spotty at best. Asking questions and pressing for accountability is often seen as an overreaction until tragedy strikes. Thankfully, it hasn’t in this case. But what can we expect the next time the sport is forced to confront events that should serve as a reminder that some things are bigger than football?

On Saturday, Air Force Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson inadvertently plunged nearly 150 feet from the Alamodome rafters onto the field during a pregame ceremony for the University of Texas at San Antonio’s matchup with Navy. He died. The game wasn’t canceled. Instead, it was delayed by roughly 10 minutes, then went on.

The Eagles’ medical staff is under the microscope. How did they determine “qualified,” and how much say did the man who had to play with minimal rest and a blood clot have in the decision? The difference between medically cleared and what’s actually safe is where the most critical juncture lives.

“Oftentimes, we want to catch these things kind of early,” Dr. Jordan Schaefer, a hematologist at the University of Michigan Health System and associate professor of internal medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School, told USA Today.

“It can get, potentially, worse.”

It did. Thankfully, not fatally worse. Nevertheless, in some London hospital, the face of a $10 billion organization sat in a room wondering how his football future and life would be affected.

You can’t just say a franchise quarterback had a blood clot, played an NFL game on a few hours of rest, then developed multiple clots in his lungs — and no one is to blame. As details continue to emerge, it becomes increasingly difficult to shake the notion that Hurts’ safety was treated more like a luxury than a priority.

Given the stakes, Hurts’ well-being shouldn’t have been something to gamble with, just another factor weighed against the cost of playing a backup. The Philadelphia Eagles have to answer for why that was ever up for debate.

title: NFL Week 7 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips - ESPN
authors: Jeremy Fowler, Dan Graziano, Nick Wagoner, Jenna Laine, ESPN staff, Mackenzie Kraemer, Tristan H. Cockcroft, Doug Greenberg, Eric Karabell, Ben Solak
description:
Insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.
Fowler: Hurts belongs high on the list, as it's worth wondering whether he has played his last down as an Eagle.
Money is a hurdle: Taylor's salaries of $9.49 million in 2026 and $20.5 million in 2027 are guaranteed.
Hurts' team considered Eagles GM Howie Roseman, specifically, "exceptional" throughout the process when it came to Hurts' health, per a source.
One consideration: The Giants have Houston (and its formidable pass rush) this week, followed by the bye week.
text:
Week 7 of the 2026 NFL season has arrived. Insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

What does the future hold for Bo Nix, Jalen Hurts, C.J. Stroud and other quarterbacks with looming contract situations? Who are some players who might be flying under the radar as trade candidates ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline? Will the Colts -- who just fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday -- keep making changes as they try to right the ship? And which of the NFC East teams in flux are most likely to shake things up in the coming weeks?

It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 7.

Jump to:

QB situations | Colts' next moves

Sneaky trade candidates

NFC East shake-ups | Fantasy advice

More notes, intel

What is the most intriguing quarterback contract situation for the offseason?

Graziano: I recognize that there are far more important real-life situations going on around this player right now, but for me, it's the Eagles' Jalen Hurts. He is signed through 2028, but the only guaranteed money left on his contract after this season will be $22 million of his $51.5 million salary in 2027. Regardless of how this season was to play out for Hurts and the Eagles, there was always going to be an offseason discussion about whether to extend him again -- and if so, at what level -- or look into other options.

The Eagles have some young stars coming up for extensions pretty soon, including cornerbacks Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean, and carrying a huge quarterback salary beyond this year is going to get more difficult. It's fair to wonder what impact Hurts being out for the rest of the season will have on the Eagles' decision-making.

Fowler: Hurts belongs high on the list, as it's worth wondering whether he has played his last down as an Eagle. He is 59-28 as a starter for the franchise, but Philadelphia, which is often proactive with contracts of core players, did not extend Hurts last offseason. So, it's difficult to pinpoint where things will stand three to four months from now.

But my pick is the Broncos' Bo Nix. Denver is good enough to keep winning despite Nix showing a limited ceiling. He is a quality starter but is not poised to enter the upper echelon. Confidence appears to be an issue this season, raising questions about what this player-team marriage looks like long term.

To be sure, the conditions around Nix aren't perfect. Denver is struggling to run the ball and effectively create explosive plays off play-action. He has had two playcallers this season. Nix got skewered for last week's performance versus Seattle. But Denver didn't have as big of a problem with it because it had to play conservatively in a tight game between two great defenses, as whichever team won the turnover battle was probably going to win the game. Broncos coach Sean Payton knew that and most certainly relayed it to Nix, whose struggles against the 49ers in Week 4 were considered more problematic. That said, Nix -- who broke his right ankle in January -- doesn't appear to be the runner he once was. His viability with Denver might hinge on how he plays over the next 11 or so games.

Graziano: I did have someone last week tell me the big difference with Nix was that he's not getting himself out of bad spots with his legs the way he did last season but that he doesn't look much different otherwise. But that lack of running is a big deal, and if it doesn't improve, we could be left watching his flaws the rest of the way.

I'm a bit curious about Sam Darnold's situation, as he'll have one year left on his contract after this season. He is scheduled to make $35.5 million in 2027, but none of that money is guaranteed. There is a $10 million roster bonus that vests on the fifth day of the league year (March 16), so the Seahawks will want to decide by then whether they want him on next year's team. But if they do, they'd also look to extend him beyond that.

What's interesting to me is that this is a different setup than Darnold had last offseason, when $17.5 million of his 2026 compensation became guaranteed on the fifth day after the Super Bowl. That was a no-brainer, of course, since Seattle won the Super Bowl with him five days earlier. But if this season doesn't go as well (the Seahawks are 3-3, and only Justin Herbert has thrown more interceptions than Darnold's seven), Seattle has four more weeks to make the decision on Darnold than it did a year ago.

Fowler: It's not helping that Drew Lock has been impressive for the Seahawks, both behind the scenes and in relief of Darnold. Darnold has earned a lot of street cred with Seattle, but he must limit the turnovers, especially with the team's dominant defense.

Houston's C.J. Stroud is fueling the offseason intrigue with his excellent play. He is putting up MVP-type numbers, pacing for nearly 4,900 passing yards over a 17-game slate while registering only one interception on 219 passing attempts. Betting on himself in Year 4 should literally pay off. The Texans were willing to extend Stroud on a deal worth well above $50 million per year. But Stroud saw a bigger picture: a growing quarterback market and his place in it. Stroud and Carolina's Bryce Young both appear well-positioned for offseason negotiations. And Houston's trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. -- Stroud's teammate while at Ohio State -- amplifies the Texans' feelings on Stroud.

What's next for the Colts? Could more moves be coming?

Fowler: It feels as if everything is on the table in Indianapolis, from an eventual head coaching change to a quarterback demotion, barring an uptick in performance. Daniel Jones' play -- 30th in QBR (38.2) with 1.5 turnovers per game -- is unsustainable over a 17-game season. This situation mirrors that of the 2025 Dolphins, who fired general manager Chris Grier in October but evaluated coach Mike McDaniel over the remainder of the season, only to fire him four days after Week 18. Miami also benched a quarterback with a high-priced contract in Tua Tagovailoa late in the campaign.

The sentiment as of now is that Colts coach Shane Steichen will get more chances to state his case for the job moving forward. But typically, franchises like to synchronize their brain trust on similar timelines, often with a newly appointed general manager spearheading a search for the new coach. That might not bode well for Steichen, whose acumen never has been questioned. He'd be in the mix for head coaching jobs or primo playcaller positions in the 2027 cycle. I'm curious about your take, Dan, but I believe team owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon plans to place her stamp on the franchise in a big way over the coming months.

Graziano: I would agree that while Steichen is well-regarded and well-liked in the building, this is definitely a situation worth monitoring for potential change at the end of the season, if not sooner. Firing a GM in mid-October indicates disappointment from ownership, obviously, but it also signals the possibility of major change on the roster, maybe even in the next few weeks. The NFL trade deadline is Nov. 10 -- less than three weeks from now -- and the Colts have a very interesting roster. There were a number of veterans who could have received contract extensions this past offseason, and the only one who got one was running back Jonathan Taylor.

High-profile veteran players such as offensive lineman Quenton Nelson, defensive linemen DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart, and wide receivers Josh Downs and Keenan Allen are on contracts that expire at the end of the season. If the Colts (who are without a 2027 first-round pick as a result of last year's Sauce Gardner trade) want to try to regain some draft capital, they could look to deal some players who they don't view as part of their future. Depending on the extent of that dealing, it could get even more difficult for Steichen to win games in the second half of the campaign, which would make it harder to convince the Colts to keep him around.

Fowler: Rival teams believe Indianapolis will be open for business ahead of the trade deadline, but for now, let's take Irsay-Gordon at her word. The last sentence from her statement Monday announcing GM Chris Ballard's firing read: "We have a lot of football in front of us, and I expect us to compete, improve and win football games." That puts Indy on a three-week clock, with the Vikings, Jaguars and Cowboys on the schedule between now and Nov. 8, two days before the deadline.

If Indy can find a way to steal two wins in that slate, perhaps that affects trade plans. But this iteration of the Colts does not look poised for upsets, so perhaps change is inevitable. What Indianapolis does with Nelson will be fascinating. He's a legacy Colt, a 2018 first-round draft pick and eight-time All-Pro. But the team did not aggressively pursue an extension this summer and rarely do premier O-linemen become available at the deadline. Also, defensive tackle Jerry Tillery is a name to watch.

Graziano: The new GM hire will be the first major organizational structure move since Irsay-Gordon took over as controlling owner, and it's even more significant if it is coupled with a coaching hire. You have a team that looks as if it will be in the offseason quarterback market, but it doesn't have a first-round pick, so the Colts might have to pursue unconventional ways of fixing their biggest roster problem of the past decade. How the Colts' decision-making structure comes together will be watched very closely around the league, as Irsay-Gordon is an unknown in terms of how she wants the team to operate and could be a very different type of decision-maker than her late father.

Who is a sleeper name for the trade deadline we're not talking about enough (or at all)?

Graziano: Tampa Bay defensive tackle Vita Vea. The Buccaneers are 1-5. Vea is 31 years old, and he and the team begrudgingly came to a compromise agreement on his contract during training camp. The Bucs didn't act as if he was part of their long-term future, and if teams come looking for a big, run-stuffing defensive tackle, Tampa would be silly not to listen. He is on a minimum salary this year and is guaranteed $23 million for 2027, which would rank about 15th in terms of cap numbers for defensive tackles in the league. If you need interior D-line help right now and don't mind paying Vea $23 million next season at age 32, why not call to see what it would take to get him out of Tampa?

Fowler: Tennessee cornerback Alontae Taylor. He was widely considered the top corner in free agency, signing a three-year, $58 million deal with the Titans in March. His Week 6 benching has placed him on the radar of teams that might look to bolster the position in the next few weeks. He has struggled as an outside corner for Tennessee but is at his best as a disruptive slot closer to the action. He's 27 with good football left, so a trade could bring out his best.

Money is a hurdle: Taylor's salaries of $9.49 million in 2026 and $20.5 million in 2027 are guaranteed. Perhaps a new team could rework that money on a new deal while asking Tennessee to front some of the bill in exchange for a quality pick. Tennessee has the option to smooth things out with Taylor and solidify a role for him -- and I don't believe the Titans are floating his name right now -- but a benching typically signals that a player is expendable.

Graziano: Interesting concept, the idea of a team trading a player so soon after signing him. It kind of reminds me of the Jets trading Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline a few months after extending his contract. Sometimes, circumstances change or things don't work out as expected, so teams will pivot if the terms are favorable. A couple of other 2026 free agent signings who stand out as potentially available due to their situations not working out include Texans offensive lineman Wyatt Teller and Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen.

Fowler: One surprise name a few teams are tracking is Cincinnati edge rusher Shemar Stewart. The 2025 first-round pick is not a factor in the team's rotation right now. He has played 17 defensive snaps, well behind the total for the fourth defensive end, Cedric Johnson (83). And rookie second-rounder Cashius Howell has been impressive. Cincinnati typically doesn't move its young draft picks, but it would be surprising if the Bengals haven't received inquiries on Stewart, whose upside remains high.

Also, could a team pry safety Jessie Bates III out of Atlanta? He will be a free agent in 2027, and the Falcons are sitting at 2-4. I doubt Atlanta wants to trade him, but his value would be strong if that changes.

Which NFC East team is most likely to shake things up in the coming weeks?

Fowler: I'll start with the Eagles. They come up most often regarding potential moves over the next few weeks. The Eagles are always active, and they could execute a mini-rebuild. Defensive end Moro Ojomo, a 2027 free agent, has strong trade value, so if Philadelphia isn't going to re-sign him, it could get compensatory pick value (or better) for him now. Woolen and wide receiver Hollywood Brown are players teams are watching.

I'm not wholly convinced the Eagles will move a marquee name such as Saquon Barkley. But can they find a taker for guard Landon Dickerson, who appears disgruntled and remains on injured reserve? The Eagles have been forced to reshape their once-vaunted offensive line on the fly, and that could facilitate moves. It's also worth noting that Philly is in the middle of a quarterback shake-up due to Jalen Hurts' absence, and recently acquired QB Joe Milton is a name to watch. The Eagles are struggling mightily to run the ball, and Milton has mobility. He could be worth looking at soon.

Graziano: The Giants could be shaking things up at quarterback, too, should they decide to give J.J. McCarthy the start this week at Houston or after their Week 8 bye. (Update: They announced Wednesday they will turn to McCarthy for Week 7.) They'd also love to alter things at running back, apparently. The new coaching staff has clearly soured on Cam Skattebo, the Giants just released Najee Harris, and it wouldn't be shocking to see them add someone from the outside or give Tyrone Tracy Jr. a bigger chance.

I'm curious to see whether Washington dips back into the wide receiver market in the wake of Terry McLaurin's injury. The Commanders are 1-4-1, which might make them seem ready to unload talent. But they're only two games out of first place, and it feels like jobs might be on the line in Washington, so they might decide they need to go for it.

Fowler: The Cowboys might have one more move in them. Perhaps that's shortsighted, given their 2-4 record. But that might as well be 4-4 in this season's NFC East climate, where no commodity is proven and Philly's transitional state has cracked the door open. As one team exec pointed out to me Tuesday, Josh Sweat to Dallas makes a lot of sense. He fits Dallas' profile, and the Cowboys need edge-rush help. Sweat's Cardinals won Sunday, but they are not contention-adjacent just yet. Sweat has been linked to the Packers, too, but Green Bay has Micah Parsons returning eventually.

Graziano: Due to prior trades, Dallas has only four picks in next year's draft and is without its second-round pick in 2028, which could make deadline dealing difficult. But the Cowboys have been uncharacteristically aggressive over the past 12 months, and they're right in the thick of the division race in spite of how poorly they've played so far. They need edge-rush help, as you pointed out, and outside of the defensive tackles, it's an extremely young defense that might benefit from a Super Bowl-winning veteran such as Sweat. The Cowboys always seem to do something this time of year, though it's possible the Joey Porter Jr. trade was their very early big in-season move.

What is your best piece of fantasy football advice for this week?

Graziano: Check to see if anyone in your league dropped Vikings running back Jordan Mason when he went on injured reserve in Week 2. Veteran Aaron Jones Sr. has held the fort and taken on a large workload, but the Vikings really believed this offseason that Mason was a back who could thrive in their redesigned run game. He'll get a chance to be their lead ball carrier, whether it's this week or in the weeks to come, and Minnesota has one of the most favorable remaining schedules for fantasy running backs in the entire league.

Fowler: Snag Washington tight end Chig Okonkwo off waivers. The Terry McLaurin injury enhances Okonkwo's value. Okonkwo and Jayden Daniels seem to have easy chemistry, resulting in 11 catches for 129 yards over the past two weeks. Okonkwo caught all seven of his targets Monday in San Francisco. He's still looking for his first touchdown this season, but that's a matter of time based on the way he's playing.

What else are you hearing this week?

Fowler: The Jalen Hurts story continues to dominate the NFL. While NFL owners staunchly defended the Eagles' handling of the blood clot issue, the NFLPA has called for a "full investigation." Here are a few nuggets to add to the situation.

Hurts visited specialists last week upon return from the London game, including a trip to Boston to see one Friday, per sources. That was part of Hurts' fact-finding process as he was ultimately placed on injured reserve the next day. Hurts' team considered Eagles GM Howie Roseman, specifically, "exceptional" throughout the process when it came to Hurts' health, per a source. He was "extremely hands on" throughout and "worried about Jalen's health more than anything else," the source added. That doesn't mean this process was easy for the Eagles, who took public scrutiny early this week. As one source said, the Eagles "were made to look like they put his life in jeopardy and that's simply not the case."

Some with the team didn't know the full extent of the situation Saturday in London. One source recalled Hurts wasn't on the team bus on the way to the stadium Saturday, presumably for a walk-through, and coaches and players knew he was dealing with something calf-related but that he was likely to play. Hurts received "state-of-the-art imaging" in London, per NFL chief medical officer Dr. Allen Sills, referring to the ultrasound Hurts received before the game.

Graziano: The NFLPA's Tuesday night statement calling for a "full investigation" into the Hurts situation underscores how odd the whole thing feels. NFL officials at the October league meeting spent Tuesday afternoon insisting the situation was handled correctly and the Eagles were not to blame for any sort of negligence regarding Hurts' health. The union, which has been gathering information on this situation over the past week, was taken aback by the speed with which the league claims to have investigated it and cleared the Eagles. Some concussion-protocol inquiries have taken weeks to complete, and the NFL is saying this very unusual situation has been examined and settled in about two days. So expect the union to continue to press for answers.

One of the things that seems so odd about this situation, though, is the extent to which Hurts' agent and the Eagles are aligned on the messaging. If Hurts and/or his representation felt the Eagles had been negligent, one imagines they would be raising hell at least behind the scenes. Instead, the agent signed off on a joint statement with the team Monday about Hurts' care and his health. We haven't heard from Hurts himself since that statement, but it's no stretch to assume the agent's stance reflects Hurts' own feelings about the situation.

Ultimately, it's a good thing the NFLPA is pushing for more transparency into what happened with Hurts, since that's the union's job -- and the league's position Tuesday didn't go much beyond, "Everything was handled fine, trust us." The union is currently waiting to hear back from the league regarding its request for a full investigation. In the meantime, the NFL or the Eagles absolutely could set up a news conference with a doctor or a member of the team's medical staff who has firsthand knowledge of Hurts' condition and the details of how he was treated -- it's not a HIPAA violation if Hurts gives them permission to discuss his condition publicly. But the fact that Hurts (via his representation), the Eagles and the NFL are all together on their messaging indicates the strong possibility that we won't get that.

Fowler: The future of the Chargers' coaching staff is a big talking point this week. Head coach Jim Harbaugh hasn't tweaked his offensive staff as of yet. Change, in some form, feels inevitable, but offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel was part of practice Tuesday. The bigger question looms: What do the Chargers do with Harbaugh if the season continues to sink? It's not the Chargers' style to pay a coach millions to not coach. But as a few industry sources pointed out, a bottom-of-the-league finish would force the Chargers to do some soul-searching, in part because the Chargers don't bring in as much revenue for their home games as other teams do, because they don't own their home stadium. Maintaining excitement is important in that regard.

Harbaugh is coming off back-to-back 11-win seasons, which typically fosters a grace period to manage the low points. That might be the case here. But if the Chargers can't turn things around and are looking at a 3-14 finish, then what?

Graziano: I do not expect the Rams to go down without a fight, and my understanding is that they will at least explore the possibility of trading for a wide receiver in the wake of Davante Adams' hamstring injury, which is expected to sideline him six to 10 weeks. The issue, of course, is that they don't have a ton to trade. They are without their first-round pick in the 2027 draft as a result of the Myles Garrett trade. They are without their third-round pick in that same draft as a result of the Trent McDuffie trade. And they're missing their second-round pick in 2028 and their third-round pick in 2029, both also as a result of the Garrett trade.

Could the Rams make a player-for-player swap of some sort? Would a team be interested in backup QB Stetson Bennett IV if the Rams decide rookie Ty Simpson is ready to be Matthew Stafford's backup? (Todd Monken coached Bennett in college -- I'm just saying.) Anyway, even with a 2-4 record, four games out of first place in their division, Adams out and Garrett likely out another two or three weeks at least, this is a Rams team that had the highest of hopes for 2026 and still believes it can play well enough to salvage this season.

Fowler: NFL coaches can be on the right or wrong side of a lethal combination: the threat of a ball spot at the 35-yard line on a kickoff touchback, and kickers who can make 50- to 60-yarders with relative ease. Defensive coordinators have been concerned about this dynamic since the league voted to adjust the touchback from the 30- to the 35-yard line. And that threat is playing out this season. Both the Cowboys and Eagles lost games on the opponent's last-second field goals despite kicking off with less than nine seconds left in regulation.

Dallas kicked the ball out of the end zone, and the Ravens needed one passing play to get in field goal range for the Week 3 win. Jacksonville's Ameer Abdullah returned Philadelphia's kick 53 yards to set up the winning kick for the Jaguars in Week 5. NFL vice president of football operations Troy Vincent remembers when teams needed roughly 30 seconds and one timeout to reach scoring range. Now, they need just a few seconds. "It has become a strategic play for the head coach -- do I kick it in the end zone or do I pick my poison and kick it to my returners?" Vincent said. "This is a real play. It is changing the outcome of football games." ESPN's Stephen Holder wrote at length about this year's wild late-game endings and how they're challenging coaches.

Also on the NFL competition front, fumbles are up about 50 from this time last year. The "Peanut punch," made famous by former Bears cornerback Charles "Peanut" Tillman, is creating more fumbles each week. Don't expect any short-term changes to help offensive players. "Ball security means everything in this game. The onus is on the player to protect that ball," said Vincent, who added the Peanut punch is something defensive players are practicing every day.

Graziano: As mentioned, the only prominent Colts veteran who got a contract extension this offseason was running back Jonathan Taylor, who is making $23 million this year, including the $15 million signing bonus he got when he signed that deal. If, hypothetically, someone wanted to trade for Taylor, the recency of the extension doesn't make it impossible for the Colts to move him, as it might in the case of some other extensions.

The Colts would have to account for $10 million of additional dead money accelerating onto their 2027 salary cap as a result of the signing bonus proration that remains. His 2026 salary is $6.98 million, so an acquiring team would be responsible for whatever percentage of that remains, plus $60,000 for each remaining game in the form of fully guaranteed per-game roster bonuses. If a team with 11 games remaining in its season were to trade for Taylor today, that team would be on the hook for about $5.3 million for 2026. Taylor is scheduled to earn another $16.02 million in 2027. None of the 2027 money is currently guaranteed, but it all becomes guaranteed five days after the Super Bowl.

And since we're on the topic and people around the league are wondering whether the Eagles would move Saquon Barkley if they decide to be deadline dealers, here's the contract impact of a hypothetical Barkley trade: The Eagles are paying him $16,750,100 this year, but $15,450,100 of that has already been paid by Philadelphia in the form of option and workout bonuses. The acquiring team would be responsible for only a prorated portion of his $1.3 million veteran-minimum salary; so acquiring him today would put you on the hook for about $867,000 in salary for the rest of this season. The Eagles would have to take a dead-money cap charge of a little more than $26 million in 2027. He's owed $16 million for 2027, of which only $2.5 million is guaranteed at this point.

So he'd be a low-risk acquisition from a financial standpoint, which tells us the Eagles could demand a very high price if they decided to move him.

Fowler: We talked about Dallas earlier. A source told me a trade to aid the Cowboys' defense is not a front-burner issue at the moment. So Dallas will always explore a potential move, but it's quite possible the franchise holds on to whatever 2027 draft capital it has left (just three picks in the first six rounds).

The Giants are not discounting J.J. McCarthy's 243-yard performance Sunday as garbage-time stat accumulation but rather an impressive performance that sets him up well in lineup considerations. The Giants are in the process of deciding whether to start McCarthy or veteran Jameis Winston. One consideration: The Giants have Houston (and its formidable pass rush) this week, followed by the bye week. Do they give McCarthy another week to learn the system and turn the keys over during the bye? That's at least a consideration. The flip side ... why wait? (Update: The Giants announced on Wednesday that they would turn to McCarthy for Week 7.)

Bears guard Jonah Jackson is dealing with a hip flexor strain that could keep him out for Thursday night, but he is practicing in a limited capacity this week. He shouldn't miss significant time. Similarly, Saints guard Cesar Ruiz's knee injury does not appear serious, per a source.

text:
The NFL Players Association is calling for full investigation into the Philadelphia Eagles' handling of quarterback Jalen Hurts’ blood clots after the NFL defended the way the situation was managed.

The NFL Players Association said it is not aware of any league investigation into the medical care provided Hurts, adding that the NFL previously told the union it did not plan to review the care he received.

“Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred,” the NFLPA said. “Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward.”

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell responded to the call for an investigation at a press conference on Wednesday.

"We welcome that," Goodell said. "That's part of our processes. That's fine."

"Obviously there was a medical evaluation, and I think our protocols were incredibly good there," he said, adding that "the most important thing here is Jalen's health."

He continued, "The protocols were followed. Our process is to make sure that's the case, and our chief medical officer has gone through that," referencing Dr. Allan Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer.

Sills said in a press conference Tuesday, "the notion that there's external factors that any of our physicians would put a player in harm's way -- that's nonsense."

"If you're not sitting in that room with that patient, and you don't have all the data, if you are speculating as a physician what should have been done, you are unprofessional and unethical in doing that,” Sills continued.

Sills says the league tracks blood clots every season, and has for at least the past ten years, and they share the data with the players' association, adding that there are a handful of clotting cases every year.

"It's not a novel situation," said Sills.

Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni defended the team's handling of Jalen Hurts' medical condition at a press conference on Monday, where he faced questions about the team's decision to play him on Oct. 11 despite knowing he had reportedly gotten little sleep after spending much of the night in the hospital.

Hurts, 28, will not be able to participate in football activities while he is on blood thinner medications to treat blood clots in both his lungs, the team said in a joint statement with Hurts' agent Monday.

The statement did not provide a timeline for the Super Bowl-winning quarterback's return to the field.

"The health of our players is always at the forefront of our mind," Sirianni said.

Sources told ESPN that Hurts was hospitalized in London until 4 a.m. on Sunday, before the Eagles played the Jacksonville Jaguars in the international game on Oct. 11.

Hurts eventually played against Jacksonville later that day, three days after reporting the injury to medical staff following practice. Specialists in London initially diagnosed him with a superficial vein thrombosis in his left calf.

Deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, is when a blood clot develops in the deep veins, usually in the legs. A pulmonary embolism, or PE, may occur when a part of the DVT clot breaks off and travels to the lungs, which can be life-threatening, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Flying with a blood clot is not always prohibited, but prolonged sitting during air travel can increase the risk of blood clots. The CDC recommends travelers at risk move around frequently and exercise their legs during long flights. Whether someone with an existing clot can safely fly depends on their individual medical circumstances.

Sirianni said the decision to play Hurts was left up to the team's medical experts.

"I'm a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them. It's not just me that has major care for our players; it's them as well," Sirianni added.

Sirianni repeatedly expressed confidence in the team's medical staff, saying "the same doctors and trainers that helped 21 of our 22 starters be available in the Super Bowl are the same guys today that deeply care about our guys to help them."

The Eagles head coach also faced questions about the decision to fly Hurts home despite knowing about a blood clot.

"We get medical information from our guys, and we always put the players' health first and foremost in every situation," he said.
